title: Signature Claim Splitter
body:
The Signature Claim Splitter is an original Signature design for the first step of verification. It takes an AI answer and splits it into single claims, each in plain words, with a marker for whether the claim matters to your decision. It does not judge truth; it makes judgement possible, by turning a smooth paragraph into a list that can be checked one item at a time. It is a design, not a public product, and it is presented as such.

How to do it: Split the answer into single claims in plain words; Mark each claim as decision-relevant or decoration; Keep the original wording alongside each plain restatement; Flag claims that changed meaning when restated; Export the list for checking by source, recomputation, or second path.

What to check: Test the Splitter on an answer you already know contains an error, and confirm the error appears as its own claim rather than hiding inside a paragraph. A splitter that preserves smooth paragraphs has not split anything.

When to stop or get help: Do not act on an answer whose decision-relevant claims remain unsplit or unverified. Use the split list as the work plan, not as a conclusion.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

title: Signature Source Opener
body:
The Signature Source Opener is an original Signature design for citation checking. It takes each listed source, opens it, finds the passage that supposedly supports the claim, and reports whether the passage matches, contradicts, or is missing. It refuses to count a citation as support until the passage is found, because a list of links is not evidence until someone has read what they point to.

How to do it: Open each listed source directly; Find the passage for each key claim; Report match, contradiction, or missing passage for each; Record the source's date and authority; Mark claims with no supporting passage as unverified.

What to check: Test the Opener with a deliberately false citation and confirm it reports the passage as missing. An opener that trusts link text is not opening anything.

When to stop or get help: Do not quote a sourced claim the Opener could not support with a found passage. Mark it unverified and investigate further.

title: Signature Number Rechecker
body:
The Signature Number Rechecker is an original Signature design for arithmetic verification. It extracts starting figures and results from an answer, recomputes each result independently, and flags any mismatch, unit change, or undisclosed rounding. It treats numbers as the most checkable part of an answer, and therefore the part with least excuse for error.

How to do it: Extract starting figures and claimed results; Recompute each result independently; Flag mismatches, unit changes, and undisclosed rounding; Show the working so a human can follow it; Keep a log of every number checked and its verdict.

title: Signature Name-Date Verifier
body:

title: Signature Certainty Meter
body:
The Signature Certainty Meter is an original Signature design that asks an answer to show its limits. For each key claim, it records how strongly the evidence supports it, what is disputed, and what would change the answer. It turns a single confident tone into a visible range, so that a reader can see at a glance which claims deserve trust and which deserve checking.

How to do it: Rate each key claim's support separately; Record what is disputed about each claim; Record what evidence would change each claim; Display the range plainly, not as a single score; Direct checking effort to the weakest claims first.

What to check: Test the Meter on a disputed topic and confirm it shows disagreement rather than a single confident verdict. A meter that always reads high is decoration.

When to stop or get help: Do not act on a disputed claim the Meter rates as weakly supported without a second, independent source.

title: Signature Code Runner
body:
The Signature Code Runner is an original Signature design for testing code claims safely. It runs AI-generated code in a contained test space with small known inputs, compares actual output with promised output, and reports any unexpected action, such as reading or changing files beyond the test. It never runs untested code on real data, because a test space exists precisely to absorb surprises.

How to do it: Run code only in a contained test space; Use small known inputs first; Compare actual output with promised output; Report unexpected file or data actions; Test edge cases before any wider use.

What to check: Test the Runner with code that tries to change a file outside the test space, and confirm it blocks or reports the attempt. A runner that silently allows it is not contained.

When to stop or get help: Do not run AI-generated code on real data or shared systems until it has passed contained tests on sample data.

title: Signature Second-Path Engine
body:
The Signature Second-Path Engine is an original Signature design for independent checking. It solves a problem by a different method from the first answer, using a different source where possible, and compares the two results in detail. It refuses to count a repeat of the same method as a second path, because repetition reproduces errors while independence exposes them.

How to do it: Solve by a genuinely different method; Use a source independent of the first; Compare results in detail, not just headlines; Investigate the exact step where paths diverge; Record both paths for repeatability.

What to check: Test the Engine by feeding it the same method twice and confirming it rejects the second as non-independent. An engine that accepts copies is a copier, not a checker.

When to stop or get help: Do not treat agreement between two copies as verification. Require a different route before raising confidence.

title: Signature Citation Detective
body:
The Signature Citation Detective is an original Signature design for hunting invented references. It searches titles, authors, and journals separately, checks year, volume, and pages against catalogues, and reports whether the work exists and whether it supports the claim. It treats a citation as a suspect until found, which is the correct attitude for a field where plausible references can be invented fluently.

How to do it: Search title, authors, and journal separately; Check year, volume, and pages against a catalogue; Open the abstract or work and find the claimed passage; Report invented, misused, or supported for each citation; Keep the search trail for each verdict.

What to check: Test the Detective with an invented citation and confirm it reports it as not found. A detective that finds everything is not searching.

When to stop or get help: Do not cite a reference in your own work until the Detective, or your own search, has found it. Passing on an invented citation spreads the error under your name.

title: Signature Media Context Checker
body:
The Signature Media Context Checker is an original Signature design for image and media claims. It traces an image to its first appearance, checks date and place against the claim, and flags cropping, stock use, or generation that changes meaning. It treats an image as a document with a history, not as self-evident proof, because images acquire false histories faster than text does.

How to do it: Trace the image to its first appearance; Check date and place against the claim; Flag cropping, stock, or generated origin that changes meaning; Compare caption with what the image shows; Report traced, untraceable, or mismatched for each image.

What to check: Test the Checker with an image from a different event and confirm it reports a mismatch. A checker that confirms every caption is not checking context.

When to stop or get help: Do not share an image as evidence for an event until its original context matches the claim.

title: Signature Two-Source Comparator
body:
The Signature Two-Source Comparator is an original Signature design for counting confirmations honestly. It examines what evidence each source actually cites, flags identical wording that suggests copying, and counts sources by independent evidence rather than by page count. Two pages repeating one press release count as one source in its ledger, however many times the claim is repeated.

How to do it: Examine the evidence each source cites; Flag identical wording suggesting copying; Trace sources to their common origin where one exists; Count confirmations by independent evidence; Report the true confirmation count plainly.

What to check: Test the Comparator with two pages that copy one release and confirm it counts one, not two. A comparator that counts pages is a counter, not a checker.

When to stop or get help: Do not present copied agreement as independent confirmation. Count by evidence, not by repetition.

title: Signature Whole-Report Audit
body:
The Signature Whole-Report Audit is an original Signature design for checking a full document, not just single answers. It lists every decision-relevant claim, ranks them by importance, assigns a check method to each, and produces a verdict ledger: verified, unverified, or contradicted. It ends with an honest summary of what remains open, so a decision-maker can approve the verified parts without pretending the whole report is settled.

How to do it: List every decision-relevant claim; Rank claims by decision importance; Assign a check method to each claim; Record verified, unverified, or contradicted per claim; Summarise open claims before any decision.

What to check: Test the Audit on a report with one planted error in a top-ranked claim, and confirm the ledger flags it as top priority. An audit that buries important errors among trivia has failed.

When to stop or get help: Do not approve a report whose top-ranked claims remain unverified. Approve verified parts and mark the rest as open work.

title: Signature Condition Finder
body:
The Signature Condition Finder is an original Signature design for restoring the limits that general statements drop. It rewrites each claim with its conditions attached: for whom, where, when, and under what conditions it holds, and it flags absolute words such as always and never for testing. A claim that survives with its conditions attached is usable; a claim that collapses without them was never as strong as it sounded.

How to do it: Rewrite each claim with who, where, when, and conditions attached; Flag absolute words for testing; Find exceptions and counterexamples; Check whether the evidence covers the user's group; Output the narrow, supported form of each claim.

What to check: Test the Finder on a claim that is true for one group only, and confirm it narrows the claim instead of repeating it generally. A finder that repeats general claims is not finding conditions.

When to stop or get help: Do not apply a general claim to yourself until the Finder confirms its conditions cover you.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

conditions = ['adults', 'clinic setting', 'eight weeks']
supported = ['adults', 'clinic setting']
print('conditions:', conditions)
print('supported conditions:', supported)
print('missing conditions:', [c for c in conditions if c not in supported])

title: Signature Back-Translation Checker
body:
The Signature Back-Translation Checker is an original Signature design for multilingual answers. It translates a passage back into its original language, compares meanings rather than words, and checks names, numbers, and dates character by character. It treats smooth target-language prose as no evidence of fidelity, because a fluent mistranslation is still a mistranslation.

How to do it: Translate the passage back into the original language; Compare meanings, not just words; Check names, numbers, and dates character by character; Flag polite and formal forms that do not fit; Mark important documents as drafts until a human speaker checks them.

What to check: Test the Checker with a deliberately altered translation and confirm it flags the meaning change. A checker that approves every smooth translation is not comparing meanings.

When to stop or get help: Do not sign or publish an important translated document on a single machine translation. A human check is part of the document.

title: Signature Agent Audit Ledger
body:
The Signature Agent Audit Ledger is an original Signature design for supervising AI agents that act on your behalf. It records every action in order, checks each action against the original instruction, and highlights any action outside that instruction for review before approval. It keeps the ledger with the approval decision, so that later questions about what happened can be answered from the record, not from memory.

How to do it: Record every agent action in order; Check each action against the original instruction; Highlight actions outside the instruction; Require a review of highlighted actions before approval; Keep the ledger with the approval decision.

What to check: Test the Ledger with a run that includes one unapproved action, and confirm it highlights exactly that action. A ledger that highlights everything highlights nothing.

When to stop or get help: Do not approve agent work that changed money, messages, files, or accounts without reviewing the ledger. If you cannot see the log, do not approve the run.

title: Signature Verification Classroom
body:
The Signature Verification Classroom is an original Signature design for teaching the verification routine. It presents short, checkable AI answers, lets learners find the planted error with guidance, and rewards careful checking over fast answers. It keeps the routine to five memorable steps, because a routine learners cannot remember without prompting is a poster, not a skill.

How to do it: Teach five steps: list claims, check sources, recompute numbers, find a second path, mark what is open; Practise on easy, checkable claims first; Let learners find a planted error with guidance; Reward careful checking over speed; Review the routine after a real consequential use.

What to check: Test the Classroom by watching learners use the routine without prompting after practice. If they only use it when reminded, simplify the routine rather than repeating it louder.

When to stop or get help: Do not teach verification as distrust of all AI answers. Teach it as ordinary care that makes good answers usable and bad answers harmless.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway.
